subject: biology
title: Body systems working together
summary: How cells build tissues, organs and systems, and how the digestive, circulatory, respiratory and excretory systems work together to keep cells supplied.
body:
Your body is made of trillions of cells, but they do not work alone. Cells group together to form tissues, organs and body systems, and these systems constantly depend on each other. Something as simple as climbing stairs needs your digestive, circulatory, respiratory and excretory systems all working at once.

## Think of it like this

### Levels of organisation are like a footy club

A single player is like a **cell**. A group of players who all do the same job, such as the forward line, is like a **tissue**. A whole team on game day, made of forwards, midfielders and backs working together, is like an **organ**, because it combines several different tissues to do one job. The club, with its senior team, coaching staff and medical staff, is like a **body system**, and the whole league is the **organism**. Players become **specialised** too: a ruck is built for height, a small forward for speed.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* players can swap clubs or retire and be replaced, but most specialised cells stay in one place for life and cannot simply become a different cell type. A body also has no "manager" making every decision; systems are coordinated by nerves and hormones.

### The circulatory system is like Melbourne's road and delivery network

The **heart** is the depot that pushes trucks out onto the roads. **Arteries** are freeways carrying traffic away from the depot at high pressure, **veins** are the return roads heading back, and **capillaries** are the narrow side streets that reach every front door. Delivery drivers drop off glucose and oxygen and pick up rubbish (carbon dioxide and **urea**) to take to the tip: the lungs and the **kidneys**. With **double circulation**, every truck calls in at the depot twice per full trip: once to go to the lungs and once to go out to the body.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* road traffic can go both ways and choose its route, but blood flows in one direction only, kept that way by the heart's pumping and the valves in the heart and veins. Also, in capillaries nothing is "handed over": substances move by diffusion through walls only one cell thick.

### Digestion is like a school canteen prep kitchen

Food arrives in big pieces that can't be served straight away. **Mechanical digestion** is the chopping: chewing and stomach churning break food into smaller bits so there is more surface area to work on. **Chemical digestion** is the cooks, the **enzymes**, each with one task: **amylase** turns starch into glucose, **protease** turns protein into amino acids and **lipase** turns fats into fatty acids and glycerol. The serving window is the **small intestine**, whose **villi** give a huge surface area for passing nutrients into the blood.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* cooks get tired and are used up by work, but enzymes are not used up in the reactions they speed up. Kitchens also build meals up, while digestion breaks big molecules down into small ones.

### In real life

When you go for a run, you feel the systems cooperating: you breathe faster to bring in more oxygen and remove carbon dioxide, and your heart beats faster to deliver glucose and oxygen to muscle cells. Kidney dialysis machines exist because the kidneys' job of filtering urea from the blood is so vital that when kidneys fail, a machine has to do it instead.

## Key ideas

### Levels of organisation

Multicellular organisms are organised in levels, from smallest to largest:

1. **Cell** — the basic unit of life, for example a muscle cell.
2. **Tissue** — a group of similar cells working together to do one job, for example muscle tissue.
3. **Organ** — a structure made of several different tissues working together, for example the stomach (muscle tissue, lining tissue, nerve tissue and blood).
4. **Body system** (organ system) — a group of organs working together to carry out a major function, for example the digestive system.
5. **Organism** — the whole living thing, made of all its systems.

Cells in a multicellular organism become **specialised**, meaning they develop features to do one job well, such as long nerve cells that carry messages over distance.

### The digestive system

The **digestive system** breaks large food molecules into small molecules that can be absorbed into the blood. **Digestion** happens in two ways:

- **Mechanical digestion**: physically breaking food into smaller pieces (chewing, the churning of the stomach). This increases surface area for enzymes.
- **Chemical digestion**: **enzymes** (proteins that speed up chemical reactions) break large molecules into small ones.

| Food molecule | Broken down into | Enzyme example |
|---|---|---|
| Starch (carbohydrate) | Glucose (sugars) | Amylase |
| Protein | Amino acids | Protease (e.g. pepsin) |
| Fats (lipids) | Fatty acids and glycerol | Lipase |

The pathway: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus. The liver makes **bile**, which breaks fat into small droplets, and the pancreas releases enzymes into the small intestine.

Most absorption happens in the **small intestine**. Its lining is covered in millions of finger-like folds called **villi**, which give a huge surface area. Each villus has thin walls and a rich blood supply, so digested nutrients pass quickly into the blood. The large intestine mainly absorbs water.

### The circulatory system

The **circulatory system** is the body's transport system. It is made of the **heart**, **blood vessels** and **blood**.

- **Arteries** carry blood away from the heart. They have thick, muscular, stretchy walls because blood is under high pressure.
- **Veins** carry blood back to the heart. They have thinner walls and valves to stop blood flowing backwards.
- **Capillaries** are tiny vessels with walls only one cell thick, so substances can diffuse between blood and cells.

Blood is made of plasma (carries dissolved glucose, carbon dioxide, urea and hormones), red blood cells (carry oxygen), white blood cells (fight infection) and platelets (help clotting).

Humans have a **double circulation**: blood passes through the heart twice for each full trip around the body. The right side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs to collect oxygen; the left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body. The left side has a thicker muscle wall because it pumps blood further.

### The respiratory system

The **respiratory system** brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide. Air travels: nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → **alveoli** (tiny air sacs).

**Gas exchange** happens in the alveoli by diffusion. Oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood in the capillaries, and carbon dioxide diffuses the other way. Alveoli are well suited to this because they:

- have a very large total surface area
- have walls only one cell thick, so the distance is short
- are surrounded by many capillaries, keeping a steep concentration gradient
- are moist, so gases can dissolve.

Breathing is driven by the **diaphragm** (a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs) and the rib muscles.

Do not mix up breathing with **cellular respiration**, the chemical reaction in mitochondria that releases energy:

`glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy)`

### The excretory system

**Excretion** is the removal of wastes made by the body's own chemical reactions. Carbon dioxide is excreted by the lungs. **Urea**, a waste made in the liver when spare amino acids are broken down, is removed by the **kidneys**.

The **excretory (urinary) system** includes the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra. The kidneys filter blood, remove urea, extra water and extra salts, and return useful substances such as glucose to the blood. The waste liquid, **urine**, travels down the ureters to the bladder.

Note: getting rid of undigested food (faeces) is called **egestion**, not excretion, because that material was never made by body cells.

### How the systems work together

Think about a cell in your leg muscle during exercise:

- The **digestive system** supplies glucose, absorbed into the blood in the small intestine.
- The **respiratory system** supplies oxygen through the alveoli.
- The **circulatory system** carries the glucose and oxygen to the muscle cell, where the mitochondria use them in cellular respiration.
- The circulatory system then carries carbon dioxide back to the lungs to be breathed out, and carries urea to the kidneys.
- The **excretory system** removes urea and balances water.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Organising levels

Place these in order from smallest to largest: stomach, digestive system, smooth muscle cell, muscle tissue.

1. A single smooth muscle cell is the smallest unit.
2. Many of these cells together form muscle tissue.
3. Muscle tissue combines with other tissues to form the stomach, an organ.
4. The stomach works with other organs in the digestive system.

Answer: smooth muscle cell → muscle tissue → stomach → digestive system.

### Example 2: Exercise data

A student measures her breathing rate and heart rate at rest and after running.

| | At rest | After running |
|---|---|---|
| Breathing rate (breaths per minute) | 14 | 32 |
| Heart rate (beats per minute) | 70 | 150 |

Explain the results.

1. During running, muscle cells carry out more cellular respiration to release more energy.
2. This needs more oxygen and produces more carbon dioxide.
3. Breathing rate rises to bring more oxygen into the alveoli and remove carbon dioxide faster.
4. Heart rate rises so blood carries oxygen and glucose to the muscles, and carbon dioxide away, more quickly.
5. This shows the respiratory and circulatory systems working together.

## Common mistakes

- Confusing breathing (moving air in and out) with cellular respiration (the reaction that releases energy).
- Saying arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood. Arteries carry blood away from the heart; the artery to the lungs carries oxygen-poor blood.
- Calling the removal of faeces "excretion". It is egestion.
- Saying a tissue is "a group of organs". A tissue is a group of similar cells.

## Exam tips

- Questions on how systems interact reward a clear chain: name each system, what it supplies or removes, and how the blood links them.
- When describing adaptations (villi, alveoli, capillaries), link each feature to its effect, such as "thin walls give a short diffusion distance".

## Tips to remember

- **Levels of organisation, a made-up trick: "Cool Teens Often Sing Out"** – Cell → Tissue → Organ → System → Organism.
- **Arteries go Away from the heart.** Veins bring blood back and have valves to stop backflow.
- **Breathing ≠ respiration.** Breathing moves air in and out. Cellular respiration is the reaction in mitochondria: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy).
- **Excretion = waste from the body's own reactions** (urea, CO₂). **Egestion = getting rid of food that was never digested** (faeces).
- **The "exchange surface" trio:** villi, alveoli and capillaries all win with a large surface area, thin walls and a good blood supply.
- **Enzyme names give a hint:** amylase breaks starch into glucose, protease breaks protein into amino acids, and lipase breaks lipids (fats) into fatty acids and glycerol.

## Key terms

- **Tissue** — a group of similar cells doing the same job.
- **Organ** — a structure made of different tissues working together.
- **Body system** — a group of organs carrying out a major function.
- **Enzyme** — a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction.
- **Villi** — finger-like folds in the small intestine that increase surface area for absorption.
- **Capillary** — a tiny blood vessel with walls one cell thick.
- **Alveoli** — tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange happens.
- **Excretion** — removal of wastes made by the body's own chemical reactions.
- **Urea** — a nitrogen-containing waste made in the liver and removed by the kidneys.

## Summary

- Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form body systems, and systems form an organism.
- The digestive system breaks food into small molecules that are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine.
- The circulatory system transports substances; the respiratory system exchanges gases in the alveoli.
- The kidneys excrete urea and control water levels.
- All systems depend on each other to supply cells with glucose and oxygen and remove wastes.

questions.prompt: Which list is in the correct order from smallest to largest?
questions.explanation: Similar cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form systems. B is tempting because an organ seems small, but an organ is made of several tissues, so tissue comes before organ.

questions.prompt: Where does most absorption of digested food into the blood take place?
questions.explanation: The small intestine has millions of villi with a huge surface area and rich blood supply. C is tempting because it is also part of the intestine, but the large intestine mainly absorbs water, not nutrients.

questions.prompt: Which feature of capillaries best allows substances to move between blood and body cells?
questions.explanation: Thin walls give a very short diffusion distance between blood and cells. A is tempting because arteries have thick walls, but thick walls would slow diffusion; they suit arteries for high pressure, not exchange.

questions.prompt: Why is the left side of the heart's muscle wall thicker than the right side?

options.A: It pumps blood to the lungs, which are further away.
options.B: It pumps blood around the whole body, which needs more force.
options.C: It carries oxygen-poor blood, which is thicker.

questions.explanation: The left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the whole body, a much longer journey, so it needs stronger muscle. A is the tempting mix-up: the right side pumps to the lungs, which are close by.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of excretion?

options.C: Breathing out carbon dioxide from the lungs
options.D: Absorbing water in the large intestine

questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is a waste made by cellular respiration in body cells, so removing it is excretion. A is tempting, but faeces is mostly undigested food that was never made by body cells, so removing it is egestion.

questions.prompt: A protein molecule in a meal is fully digested. What is it broken down into?
questions.explanation: Protease enzymes break proteins into amino acids. D is tempting because urea is made from amino acids, but that happens later in the liver when spare amino acids are broken down, not during digestion.

questions.prompt: A person's heart rate rises from 70 to 140 beats per minute during exercise. Which explanation is best?

options.A: The heart needs to pump more urea to the kidneys.
options.B: The lungs need more blood to stay moist.
options.C: Faster digestion requires more blood in the stomach.
options.D: Muscles need more oxygen and glucose for cellular respiration, and more carbon dioxide must be removed.

questions.explanation: Working muscles respire faster, so blood must deliver oxygen and glucose and remove carbon dioxide more quickly. A is tempting since blood does carry urea, but that is not the main reason heart rate rises during exercise.

questions.prompt: A disease damages the walls of the alveoli so that the total surface area is reduced. What is the most likely effect?

options.A: Less urea is removed from the blood.
options.B: Less oxygen diffuses into the blood, so the person tires easily.
options.C: More glucose is absorbed into the blood.
options.D: The person can no longer digest fats.

questions.explanation: A smaller surface area slows gas exchange, so less oxygen enters the blood and cells release less energy. A is tempting because the excretory system can be affected in the long term, but removing urea is the kidneys' job, not the lungs'.
